newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - Olympic city and capital -- can Cape Town be both?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Olympic city and capital -- can Cape Town be both?.

text.p: Winning the right to host the 2004 Olympic Games could cost South Africa's foremost tourist city its status as the seat of the country's parliament.
Cape Town, shortlisted with Athens, Buenos Aires, Rome and Stockholm will hear on September 6 whether it will become the first African venue for the Games.
About three months later it will hear whether President Nelson Mandela's ruling African National Congress (ANC) is willing to let the city remain the seat of parliament.
The question being asked is whether Cape Town, which scores highest in the country on natural beauty, living standards, economic growth and tourism, should have both the Olympics and the legislature.

Cape Town's bid committee estimates the Games could inject up to 30 billion rand ($6.6 billion) into the national economy, much of it into the city's domestic economy, create up to 100,000 permanent jobs and put the city firmly on the world tourism map.
Cape Town's Citizen's Alliance for Parliament estimates that moving the legislature could cost the country four billion rand, the city 10,000 jobs and bump Cape Town off the political map forever.

Groups pushing Pretoria and the nearby Midrand commercial and conference centre as alternative homes for the 490-member parliament are preparing to link the two decisions if Cape Town wins the 2004 Games.
"The Pretoria lobby is saying that if Cape Town wins the Olympics that's enough compensation for losing parliament," said Kallie Hanekom, Citizen's Alliance executive director.
OLYMPIC SMOKESCREEN
"Parliament will be here forever. The Olympics will come and go, but I think the enemies of Cape Town are going to use it for all they're worth. It's going to be a massive factor," he said.
A senior ANC member of parliament, speaking on condition that he was not named, agreed that advocates of a move would link the two issues if Cape Town was successful.

"There is no doubt in my mind that parliament will move -- it has to go. But if Cape Town gets the Olympics, it will make it that much easier for us to take that decision. It won't seem so much like we are taking something away from them," he said in a comment echoed by more than a dozen party colleagues.
Mandela has forbidden cabinet ministers to discuss the issue in public and ANC legislators contacted by Reuters declined to speak publicly about their preferences.
The issue is as divisive now as it was when two Boer republics and two British colonies came together in 1910 to form the Union of South Africa, now a republic.
The white founding fathers failed then to agree on a single capital, opting instead to give Pretoria the executive, Cape Town the legislature, Bloemfontein the Supreme Court and Durban a big cheque.

Last year, lawmakers writing South Africa's first permanent constitution again failed to settle on a single capital, saying Cape Town would remain the seat of parliament unless 201 of the 400 National Assembly members decided otherwise.

"This issue is more emotional than any other I have come across. Even the abortion debate was easier," said Hanekom in a reference to the acrimonious debate earlier this year that led to the legalisation of abortion.
CAPE WEIGHS SECESSION
Pretoria city councillor Peter Maluleka fanned the debate when he claimed recently to know that four senior cabinet ministers had come out in favour of a move to his city.

The ministers named all denied that they had expressed any opinion and Mandela's office issued a statement reaffirming that the decision would be taken by parliament after a process of assessment and consultation.

Western Cape provincial minister Gerald Morkel was so outraged by the report that government ministers were taking sides before the formal debate on the issue that he suggested the province with Cape Town as its capital should secede.
Mandela phoned Morkel the next day to assure him that no decision had been taken and that the process of assessment was under way.

Officially, the decision is in the hands of a cabinet committee headed by Transport Minister Mac Maharaj, an ardent advocate of moving, and including Cape Town-born Finance Minister Trevor Manuel, Constitutional Development Minister Mohammed Valli Moosa and Public Works Minister Jeff Radebe.
Unofficially, according to a number of ANC legislators, the decision is in place and all that remains is to build up a credible justification and implement the move.

"My sense is that the sentiment is overwhelmingly in favour of moving parliament to Gauteng, probably Midrand. If Cape Town doesn't get the Olympics, it might all take a little longer, but I think there is no doubt it will happen," said a black ANC legislator who prefers Cape Town.
Speaker of parliament Frene Ginwala has refused to be drawn on her preference, but she did say recently that she wanted a final decision soon to put an end to the uncertainty.

Ray Hartley, political correspondent of Johannesburg's Sunday Times, said, however, the issue was so sensitive and the arguments so finely balanced that the ANC might never be able to take the final decision needed.
"At the end of the day, the only way the ANC can continue to serve its own political interests is by reaffirming its decision to take no decision at all," he said. ($=R4.55)
